nodes.title: Comparative World Religions
nodes.description: An introduction to the comparative study of religion, focusing on religious traditions of global significance. Although historical aspects of these traditions will be studied, emphasis will be placed on religious beliefs and practices as manifested in the contemporary world.

nodes.title: Technoscience and Religion
nodes.description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the complex relationship between “technoscience,” as a broad field of inquiry into the global human practices of technology combined with scientific methods, ranging from biology to computer sciences and robotics, with religion in its complex social manifestations.

nodes.title: First-year Student Seminar in Religion
nodes.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic related to the study of religion with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.

nodes.title: Race and Religion in America
nodes.description: This course examines the intertwined histories of race and religion in the United States, exploring how religious beliefs, experiences, and institutions have shaped racial identities and hierarchies, and also how communities have used religion as a resource for resistance and justice.

nodes.title: Tools and Methods in the Study of Religion
nodes.description: This course provides an advanced introduction to assumptions and norms that shape the study of religion as an academic field; to significant debates within the field; and to tools and methods used for professional research within the field.

nodes.title: Texts and Context: East Asian Religions
nodes.description: An introduction to the religions of China and Japan, including Confucianism, Taoism, Shinto, and Buddhism.

nodes.title: Topics in Religion and Sexuality
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: How does religiosity as a significant cultural component help mold gender and sexuality identities? The class offers topical investigations into this question.

nodes.title: Topics in Orthodoxy and Heterodoxy
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Religious dogmas often develop in dialogue with alternative viewpoints that ultimately are rejected by heterodox by the dominant group. This class presents case studies in the interpretation of such ideological and sociological pairings using scriptural, literary, and analytic sources.

nodes.title: Topics in American Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Topical studies in the history of religion in American society, ranging from the Puritans to the New Age.

nodes.title: Literature and Religion
nodes.description: This course provides an introduction to the history and themes in the relationship between literature and religion from antiquity to the present. The course examines key texts in world literature such as Rumi’s Masnavi, Milton’s Paradise Lost, and Tale of the Heike. It also considers sacred texts, such as the Bhagavad Gita, Bible, Quran, and Tao Te Ching, as works of literature, and studies the relationship between literary and religious practices in various traditions.

nodes.title: Public Sphere and Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This interdisciplinary course will explore the historical and theoretical relationship between public sphere and religion, particularly focusing on the manifestation of religious power, public ritual, and sacred theatricality in everyday spaces of life.

nodes.title: Secularization and Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Surveys the relationship between religion and modernity, in particular the problematic of the secularization theory; covers cases such as Catholic liberation theology and Islamic fundamentalism, with particular focus on the “deprivatization of modern religion.”

nodes.title: Topics in Performing Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course explores religion as a system of bodily practices, rather than one of tenets or beliefs. How do day-to-day activities as well as significant rituals express and inform people’s religious lives? Why is doctrine an insufficient basis for understanding religion? May be taken up to three times as topics vary.

nodes.title: Devils and Demons in Christianity
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Christianity frequently finds definition in contradistinction to an “Other” characterized as immoral, irrational, and malevolent. This class investigates how devils and demons as constructions of the “Other” have contributed to Christianity’s growth and identity formation throughout history.

nodes.title: Communication, Technology, and Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course will look at the relationship between information communication technologies (ICTs) and religion and how they have intersected or diverged in the course of history. We will look at both older and newer media, such as telegraph, radio, television, cassette tapes, internet, and satellite, and how they have been used by groups like Evangelical, Catholic, or Islamist movements in proliferation and transformation of ideas, rituals, ideologies, values, and diverse forms of sociability. Students may not receive credit for both RELI 145 and RELI 145GS.

nodes.title: Communication, Technology, and Religion
nodes.prereq_text: students must apply and be accepted to the Global Seminars program.

nodes.description: This course will look at the relationship between information communication technologies (ICTs) and religion and how they have intersected or diverged in the course of history. We will look at both older and newer media, such as telegraph, radio, television, cassette tapes, Internet and satellite, and how they have been used by groups like evangelical, Catholic, or Islamist movements in proliferation and transformation of ideas, rituals, ideologies, values, and diverse forms of sociability. Program or materials fees may apply. Students may not receive credit for both RELI 145GS and RELI 145.

nodes.title: Topics in the Religions of Antiquity
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Topical studies in the religious beliefs, practices, and institutions of pre-Christian Europe and near East. May be repeated for credit up to three times when topics vary.

nodes.title: Pagan Europe and Its Christian Aftermath
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: (Cross-listed with HIEU 107.) This course explores the history of how western Europe was converted from its indigenous pagan religions to the imported religion we know as Christianity. We will discuss conversion by choice and by force, partial or blended conversions, and the relationships between belief and culture. Students may not receive credit for HIEU 107 and RELI 147.

nodes.title: Religion and Women’s Activisms
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The course surveys women’s formal and informal roles and activities in a number of faiths, examining how women’s agency and activism may be constrained or fostered by religious ideologies and norms in various historical and political contexts. Examples are drawn from a range of male-centered religions (Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism), woman-centered religions (Sande, Afro-Brazilian, Z-ar Cult), and newly formed theologies (Womanist, Native American, and Mujerista; New Age feminist spiritualities).

nodes.title: Islam in America
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course introduces the students to historical and social developments of Islam in the United States. Tracing Islam back to the African slaves, the course examines various Muslim communities in the United States, with a focus on African American Muslims, especially Malcolm X.

nodes.title: Religion and Cinema
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: The course is an introductory study of cinema and religion. It explores how cinema depicts religion and spiritual experience. A number of films will be studied to understand how cinematic and religious narratives and practices overlap and, at times, diverge in complex ways.

nodes.title: Deep Ecology: Knowing Place
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course explores intersections between religious discourse and ecological discourse by considering texts from both that treat the human world as irreducibly interconnected with more-than-human worlds of nature and “spirit.” Themes include the ambivalence of wildness; the critique of anthropocentrism (human-centeredness); and the question of how religious emphasis on “knowing (one’s) place” can create a sense of either human exceptionality, above nature, or embeddedness, within nature.

nodes.title: Media and Islam in the U.S.
nodes.description: This course examines histories and theories of media and Islam. It especially offers an overview on intersections between media representation and religious experience with a focus on the United States.

nodes.title: Hispanic American Religions
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course introduces students to historical and social developments of religion among Hispanic Americans. The course examines changing religious traditions and ritual practices among Hispanic Americans with a focus on Catholicism and (evangelical) Protestantism.

nodes.title: Asian American Religions
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course introduces students to historical and social developments of religion among Asian Americans. Tracing back to the mid-nineteenth century, the course examines changing religious traditions and ritual practices among Asian American communities.

nodes.title: African American Religions
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: This course introduces students to historical and social developments of religion among African Americans. The course examines changing religious traditions and ritual practices among African Americans since slavery to the present era.

nodes.title: Posthuman Spirituality
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing.
nodes.description: This course will survey questions surrounding the “coevolution” of human and technics and ways such processes are making new worlds of which we often feel a sense of perpetual disruption. We investigate posthuman not only in terms of new technological practices but spiritual experiences that bring about new understandings of being human in the world.

nodes.title: Religion in Japan
nodes.description: This course examines Japanese religions by studying various traditions including Buddhism, Christianity, and Shintoism and their influence on Japanese culture such as anime and cinema. Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program.

nodes.title: Japanese Literature and Spirituality
nodes.description: This course looks at the relationship between literature and spirituality in Japan. The course explores this relationship in the works of Shusaku Endo, Hiromi Ito, Yasunari Kawabata, Haruki Murakami, and others. Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program.

nodes.title: Native Religions
nodes.prereq_text: Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program.

requires.text: Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program

nodes.description: This course explores Native American ways of life and religions; it also examines the impact of European invasion and colonization.

nodes.title: Religion and Politics
nodes.prereq_text: Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program.

requires.text: Students must apply and be accepted into the Global Seminar Program

nodes.description: Explores the complex relationship between religion and politics in a variety of historical and social contexts. The course examines a range of texts and case studies with a focus on the intersection of religion with politics.

nodes.title: Drama, Politics, and Religion in Ancient Greece
nodes.prereq_text: Students must apply and be accepted to the Global Seminars Program.

requires.text: Students must apply and be accepted to the Global Seminars Program

nodes.description: This course examines the history of ancient Greek theatre and the importance of theatre in relation to myth, politics, and religion. Key plays by Aeschylus, Aristophanes, and Sophocles will be studied with a focus on fate, ritual, myth, and civic politics. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Special Topics in Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Students in this lecture will investigate important problems in the study of religion or the history of particular religions. RELI 188 and RELI 188GS may be taken for credit for a combined total of three times.

nodes.title: Special Topics in Religion
nodes.description: Students in this course will investigate important problems in the study of religion or the history of particular religions. Department approval required. Students must apply for and be accepted into the Global Seminars Program. RELI 188GS and RELI 188 may be taken for credit for a combined total of three times. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Seminar in Religion
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing.
nodes.description: This seminar requires the intensive analysis of critical problems in the study of religion or the history of particular religions. May be repeated for credit up to three times when topics vary.

nodes.title: Senior Seminar in Religion
nodes.description: The senior seminar is designed to allow senior undergraduates to meet with faculty members in a small group setting to explore an intellectual topic in religion at the upper-division level. Topics will vary from quarter to quarter. Senior seminars may be taken for credit up to four times, with a change in topic and permission of the department. Enrollment is limited to twenty students, with preference given to seniors.

nodes.title: Honors Thesis in Religion
nodes.prereq_text: RELI 101 (may be completed concurrently with the honors sequence). Department approval required for entry into the Honors Program.

items.text: RELI 101 (may be completed concurrently with the honors sequence)

nodes.description: First quarter of a two-quarter sequence of individualized, directed-research courses for majors in which students learn firsthand the processes and practices of scholarly research in the study of religion, culminating in the completion of a thesis and an oral presentation. Students may not receive credit for both RELI 196H and RELI 196AH.

nodes.title: Honors Thesis in Religion
nodes.prereq_text: RELI 196A. Department approval required for continuing participation in the Honors Program.
nodes.description: Second quarter of a two-quarter sequence of individualized, directed-research courses for majors in which students learn firsthand the processes and practices of scholarly research in the study of religion, culminating in the completion of a thesis and an oral presentation. Students may not receive credit for both RELI 196H and RELI 196BH.

nodes.title: Directed Advanced Readings
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing; RELI 110A or 110B; overall GPA of 2.5.
nodes.description: A faculty member will direct a student in advanced readings on a topic not generally included in the Program for the Study of Religion’s curriculum. Students must make arrangements with the program and individual faculty. May be repeated for credit up to three times for credit.

nodes.title: Independent Research Study for Undergraduates
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing, with 2.5 GPA (overall); program stamp.
nodes.description: Independent research in religion under the supervision of a faculty member affiliated with the Program for the Study of Religion. This course may be repeated three times with program approval. (P/NP grades only.)
